rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Friction is a contact force opposing relative motion. Static friction (variable, up to μ_sN) acts before sliding; kinetic friction (constant, μ_kN) acts during sliding, with μ_k < μ_s. The angle of repose equals the angle of friction (tan⁻¹μ_s). Slope problems, pulling/pushing at angles, and the distinction between static and kinetic friction are the key NEB topics.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Maximum static friction: f_s(max) = μ_sN (acts just before slipping)
Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_kN (acts during sliding; μ_k < μ_s)
Slope sliding condition: body slides when tan θ > μ_s; a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Static vs. Kinetic Threshold:** The maximum static friction $f_s^{\max} = \mu_s N$ is the *upper bound* for static friction. Static friction is a *variable* force that matches the applied force up to this limit. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ applies *only* when sliding occurs, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.  ·  **Normal Force Dependency:** Friction is proportional to the *normal reaction*, not the weight. Any vertical force component (pulling up, pushing down, incline) changes $N$, which directly changes the friction force. Always compute $N$ first.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Static friction is NOT always μ_sN — it is a variable force that matches the applied force up to that maximum.  ·  The normal force is NOT always mg — on a slope it is mg cos θ; with pulling/pushing at an angle it changes.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Slope: A 5 kg block on a 30° slope (μ_s = 0.4). tan 30° = 0.577 > 0.4 → slides. a = g(sin30° − μ_k cos30°) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.4×0.866) = 1.51 m/s².  ·  Horizontal pull: A 10 kg block (μ_k = 0.25) pulled by 40 N at 20° above horizontal. N = 98 − 40sin20° = 84.3 N; f = 21.1 N; F_net = 40cos20° − 21.1 = 16.5 N; a = 1.65 m/s².

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 slope problems: check if the body slides (tan θ vs μ_s) and find the acceleration.  ·  Solve 5 horizontal-surface problems with pulling/pushing at an angle.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Slope check: compare tan θ with μ_s — if tan θ > μ_s, the body slides; otherwise it stays.  ·  Normal force shortcut: N = mg (horizontal), N = mg cos θ (slope), N = mg − F sin θ (pulling up), N = mg + F sin θ (pushing down).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 15 kg block rests on a horizontal surface (μ_s = 0.6). What is the maximum static friction? What horizontal force is needed to just start it moving?  ·  A 5 kg block slides down a 40° slope (μ_k = 0.25). Find the acceleration.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Slope problems are the most common — know the tan θ vs μ_s check and the a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) formula.  ·  Pulling/pushing at an angle changes the normal force — always recalculate N before finding friction.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Friction is a contact force opposing relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces.  ·  Static friction is variable (up to μ_sN); kinetic friction is approximately constant (μ_kN).  ·  μ_k < μ_s — harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.  ·  The angle of repose equals the angle of friction: θ_r = λ = tan⁻¹μ_s.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN.  ·  Kinetic friction is approximately CONSTANT: f_k = μ_kN during sliding.  ·  Friction is (approximately) independent of the apparent area of contact.  ·  Pulling at an angle reduces N and friction; pushing at an angle increases both.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact — a counterintuitive but experimentally verified law.  ·  μ_k < μ_s for most surface pairs — this is why objects jerk when starting to slide.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A 10 kg block is pulled by a 50 N force at 30° above horizontal (μ_k = 0.2). Find the acceleration.  ·  A block remains at rest on a slope up to 35°. Find μ_s. If the slope is increased to 40°, find the acceleration (μ_k = 0.6).  ·  Explain why it is harder to start sliding a heavy box than to keep it sliding.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Static friction is variable — do NOT assume f = μ_sN unless the body is at the point of slipping.  ·  The angle of repose equals the angle of friction — both are tan⁻¹μ_s.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Angle of repose: A block slides at constant speed down a 35° slope. μ_k = tan 35° = 0.70. μ_s is slightly higher (≈ 0.75).  ·  Static friction variable: A 20 kg box (μ_s = 0.5). Push with 40 N — box doesn't move, f_s = 40 N. Push with 120 N — box moves (max f_s = 98 N).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **What friction is:** a contact force that opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact. It acts parallel to the contact surface. Static friction (no sliding) and kinetic friction (sliding) are the two main types.  ·  **Laws of friction:** (1) Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact (to a good approximation). (2) Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_s(max) = μ_sN, f_k = μ_kN. (3) μ_k < μ_s — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.  ·  **Static friction is a variable force:** it matches the applied force up to a maximum: f_s ≤ μ_sN. If you push with 30 N and the object doesn't move, f_s = 30 N (not μ_sN). Only at the point of slipping does f_s = μ_sN.

rows.text: • Laws of solid friction  ·  • Their verifications  ·  ❌ 'Friction always opposes motion.' ✅ Friction opposes RELATIVE motion (or its tendency). Static friction can act IN the direction of motion — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking.
